blocks.text: A chronic sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. It progresses in stages and can involve multiple organ systems if untreated.

blocks.text: Primary syphilis: Painless genital, anal, or oral ulcer (chancre) and non-tender lymphadenopathy.
Secondary syphilis: Generalized non-itchy rash (often on palms/soles), mucous patches, condylomata, fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy.
Latent syphilis: Asymptomatic; detected by serology.
Tertiary syphilis: Rare; gummatous lesions, cardiovascular or neurologic disease.
Congenital syphilis: Stillbirth, neonatal death, or multisystem disease in infants.
Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, otosyphilis: Can occur at any stage; present with neurological, visual, or auditory symptoms.
Non-treponemal: RPR, VDRL (for screening and monitoring).

Direct detection: Darkfield microscopy or NAAT from ulcer exudate/tissue (if available). CSF examination: For neurologic, ocular, or otic symptoms (cell count, protein, VDRL). HIV testing: Recommended for all patients with syphilis.

blocks.text: Syndromic approach of managing STIs/RTIs entails the service provider to follow laid down steps in a flow chart which guides him/her in making rational management decisions for treating the client. These are therefore known as treatment flow-charts. They may also be known as treatment algorithms, treatment protocols or treatment decision trees.
